normalized.governing_thought: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
executive_summary: Market: The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it. US quick-commerce GMV grew 42% a year, 2022–25. Both incumbents lose money on every order (EBITDA margins −26% and −46%); QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities.

Economics: A Parcelbird dark store would lose money on every order, and customers don't stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost. Loss of $6.17 per order at benchmark median, and $1.76 with best-observed inputs on every driver. Only the founders' plan (+$2.02) is profitable, and it beats the best site ever observed on all four drivers. Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order; 22% of its customers were still ordering in month 3.

Funding: Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints. The launch needs $9.5M; only $7.2M can be spent while keeping 12 months of runway. Adding today's core burn, cash runs out in month 13. At benchmark economics, 9 stores would lose $18M a year.

Alternative: The software business is a better use of the same cash. It breaks even in about month 26 at today's 60% growth (month 36 at 40%) and never drops below 12 months of runway, provided growth stays at 34% or more. Selling store-based fast delivery to pipeline grocers gives Parcelbird a share of the market's growth.

Decisions for the board: (1) decline the 2027 launch and do not extend the pop-up; (2) approve the $0.8M a year of software hires, phased against signed contracts; (3) build a store-based fast-delivery offer for the grocers in the pipeline; (4) adopt explicit re-entry triggers, tracked through our customers' sites, before quick commerce is reconsidered.

slides.title: We started from the founders' answer, "launch", and tested the six conditions it needs; the evidence supports none of them

claims.claim: Initial hypothesis tested: “Parcelbird should launch Parcelbird Now: 9 dark stores in 3 cities, contribution-positive per order by month 18.”
1. The market has a profit pool, not just growth — Not met
evidence: GMV +42% a year, but contribution per order is −$1.90 (Zipcart) and −$3.40 (QuickBasket); QuickBasket shut 36% of its cities

claims.claim: 2. A dark store makes money per order at achievable inputs — Not met
evidence: −$6.17 per order at benchmark median; −$1.76 even with every best-observed input combined

claims.claim: 3. Parcelbird runs stores better than the benchmark — Not shown
evidence: The pop-up was below the median on all four drivers (AOV, promotions, rider productivity, density)

claims.claim: 4. Customers stay long enough to repay acquisition cost — Not met
evidence: $38 CAC; 22% still ordering in month 3; CAC is never repaid at benchmark or pop-up economics

claims.claim: 5. The plan fits current cash with 12 months of runway — Not met
evidence: $9.5M needed vs $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; no new funding expected

claims.claim: 6. It beats the best other use of the cash — Not met
evidence: The software business can reach break-even within current cash if growth stays at 34% or more

claims.claim: So what: the hypothesis fails on every condition, so we reverse it.

slides.title: Quick commerce is growing 42% a year, but both incumbents lose money on every order and one is already retreating

claims.claim: Quick commerce is growing 42% a year
Both incumbents lose money on every order
evidence: Zipcart (national): Revenue $1,200M; EBITDA −$310M; EBITDA margin −26%; Contribution per order −$1.90
QuickBasket (regional): Revenue $210M; EBITDA −$96M; EBITDA margin −46%; Contribution per order −$3.40

claims.claim: One is already retreating
evidence: QuickBasket: Closed 4 of 11 cities (36%) in 2025
Zipcart: Positive in only its densest city, and only after a fee rise (p. 10)

claims.claim: So what: the market's growth is real, but none of it has become profit. "Nobody owns the Midwest" may simply mean nobody has made it pay. Growth does not justify entry on its own; the per-order economics have to.

slides.title: At benchmark-median inputs a Parcelbird store would lose $6.17 per order; $2.67 of that is lost before any site cost, so more volume cannot fix it

claims.claim: At benchmark-median inputs a Parcelbird store would lose $6.17 per order
evidence: Contribution per order at benchmark median (14 customer sites, 2025): Goods margin (27% × $34) +9.18; Delivery fee +1.99; Promotions (6% × $34) −2.04; Picking & packing −3.10; Rider ($17.75 ÷ 2.4) −6.03 [chart value]; Payment & packaging −1.30; Before site fixed cost −2.67; Site fixed cost ($1.15M ÷ 328.5k) −3.50; After site fixed cost −6.17

claims.claim: Each order brings in $11.17 (goods margin plus delivery fee) and costs $13.84 in promotions, picking, riders and payment before the store's rent and staff are counted.
Higher density spreads the $3.50 of site cost over more orders, but each extra order still loses $2.67. The model only turns positive if AOV or rider productivity rise sharply.
Riders: $7.40 per order, 81% of the goods margin.
evidence: Two of our three cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.

slides.title: Only the founders' plan makes money; even the best-observed result on every driver at once loses $1.76 per order

claims.claim: Only the founders' plan makes money
evidence: Contribution per order before / after site fixed cost: Columbus pop-up −6.21 / −12.57; Benchmark median −2.67 / −6.17; Best observed (all drivers) +0.49 / −1.76; Founders' plan +3.77 / +2.02
Profit per store per year: Pop-up −$1.3M; Median −$2.0M; Best obs. −$0.9M; Plan +$1.3M
Inputs: AOV / promotions $31/12%, $34/6%, $42/6%, $45/2%; orders per rider-hour 2.1, 2.4, 3.0, 3.5; orders per site per day 280, 900, 1,400, 1,800

claims.claim: No site has achieved the best-observed case
evidence: The best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 orders/day) come from different sites. Combining them is already optimistic, and it still loses money.

claims.claim: Only the plan's inputs give a profitable network.
evidence: Nine stores at network scale: Median: −$18.2M a year. Best observed: −$8.1M a year. Founders' plan: +$11.9M a year.

claims.claim: Break-even AOV
evidence: With other inputs held, the median store needs an AOV of $63 and the best-observed store $50. The median is $34 and the best ever observed is $42.

slides.title: The founders' plan needs results beyond the best site ever observed on all four drivers; if AOV or rider productivity only reaches the median, the plan loses money again

claims.claim: The founders' plan needs results beyond the best site ever observed on all four drivers
evidence: Average order value: median $34, best $42, plan $45, +7% vs best
Promotions, % of AOV: pop-up 12%, median 6%, best 6%, plan 2%, −4 pts
Orders per rider-hour: range 1.9–3.0, median 2.4, best 3.0, plan 3.5, +17% above range
Orders per site per day: range 400–1,400, median 900, best 1,400, plan 1,800, +29% above range

claims.claim: If AOV or rider productivity only reaches the median, the plan loses money again
evidence: Plan profit per order if one driver is at the median: Plan as proposed 2.02; AOV $45 → $34 −0.73; Riders 3.5 → 2.4 /hr −0.31; Orders/day 1,800 → 900 +0.22; Promotions 2% → 6% +0.27

claims.claim: Falling short on density or promotions alone still leaves a thin positive margin of about $0.2–0.3 per order, but nothing for HQ overhead or marketing.
Sanity check on scale
evidence: 9 stores × 1,800 orders × $45 × 365 days = $266M a year of sales in three mid-size cities. That is more than QuickBasket's total 2025 revenue ($210M) across all its cities, and about 5% of the entire 2025 US market ($5.1B).

slides.title: Our own Columbus pop-up came in below the benchmark median on every driver, so there is no evidence yet that we run stores better than others

claims.claim: Our own Columbus pop-up came in below the benchmark median on every driver
evidence: AOV $31 vs median $34 (−9%)
Promotions 12% vs 6% (2× higher)
Orders per rider-hour 2.1 vs 2.4 (−13%)
Orders per site per day 280 vs 900 (−69%)
Contribution before site cost −$6.21 vs −$2.67 (plan +$3.77); after site cost −$12.57 vs −$6.17 (plan +$2.02)
Pop-up site cost: $650,000 a year ÷ (280 × 365 orders) = $6.36 per order. Rider cost: $17.75 ÷ 2.1 = $8.45 per order.

claims.claim: The pop-up is the only test of this, and it did worse than the median of the stores our software runs.
evidence: Founders: "Our software already runs other people's dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone."

claims.claim: Fair caveat: it was early
evidence: Six weeks on a temporary site. Orders grew 18% a week, from roughly 179 a day in week 1 to roughly 408 in week 6 (our estimate from the compounding). But that growth came with 12% promotions and $38 of acquisition cost per customer.

claims.claim: Ramp-up alone does not close the gap.
evidence: Even if density reached the median, the store would still lose $6.17 per order (p. 5).

slides.title: Customers don't stay long enough to repay their $38 acquisition cost: 44% say they would order weekly, but only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month 3

claims.claim: 44% say they would order weekly
evidence: 44% of 1,500 surveyed Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery “at least weekly” (stated intent, one age group only)

claims.claim: only 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month 3
evidence: 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month 3, at 3.1 orders a month (observed behaviour)
0.68 orders a month per acquired customer by month 3 (22% × 3.1)

claims.claim: Customers don't stay long enough to repay their $38 acquisition cost
evidence: Columbus pop-up: −$6.21; Never; Never
Benchmark median: −$2.67; Never; Never
Best observed: +$0.49; 77 orders; 113 months (~9 years)
Founders' plan: +$3.77; 10 orders; 15 months
Months = ($38 ÷ contribution per order) ÷ 0.68 orders per acquired customer per month. This is generous: it assumes no churn after month 3 and uses contribution before any site cost.

claims.claim: So what: buying growth with promotions and paid social does not create value at these economics. At the median, every customer acquired adds to the losses. Even under the founders' plan, payback takes more than a year.

slides.title: Zipcart's one profitable city needed a $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions, and it lost 14% of its volume; the same moves on our median store still lose $1.05 per order

claims.claim: Zipcart's one profitable city needed a $3.99 fee and near-zero promotions, and it lost 14% of its volume
evidence: "Zipcart turned contribution-positive (+$0.40 per order)" was true only for its densest city, after a new $3.99 fee on every order and a cut in promotions to 1%. Volume in that city then fell 14%.

claims.claim: The same moves on our median store still lose $1.05 per order
evidence: Benchmark median −6.17; +$3.99 service fee +3.99; Promotions 6% → 1% +1.70; Volume −14%: site cost per order −0.57; With Zipcart moves −1.05

claims.claim: What it would take for us
evidence: With those moves, a median store before site cost earns +$3.02 per order. To cover $1.15M of site cost it needs about 1,042 orders a day after the fee rise: 16% above today's median, 3.7× the pop-up, and with no loss of rider productivity at the lower volume.

claims.claim: A profitable route may exist, but only at top-quartile density with premium pricing. This is not where a new entrant starts, and nothing in our data shows it yet.

slides.title: Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the 12-month runway rule, and with today's core burn added it runs out of cash by month 13

claims.claim: The launch breaks the 12-month runway rule
evidence: Cash in bank $12.0M; 12-month runway floor (12 × $0.4M) $4.8M; Spendable $7.2M; Founders' cash need to month 18 $9.5M; Shortfall $2.3M

claims.claim: With today's core burn added it runs out of cash by month 13
evidence: With software ARR still growing 60% a year, cash falls below 12 months of runway in month 5 and below zero in month 13 (model, p. 14).

claims.claim: Even if the $9.5M covered all company spending
evidence: $12.0M − $9.5M = $2.5M left at month 18: about 6 months of runway at today's burn, against the 12 required.

claims.claim: If benchmark economics apply rather than the plan's
evidence: A mature 9-store network loses about $18M a year ($1.5M a month), more than our total cash every year.
The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator "unlikely".

claims.claim: The floor rises once stores are operating, because a higher burn needs a larger reserve to cover 12 months. The $7.2M of headroom is therefore a ceiling.

slides.title: Of the three options, only software-first meets both investor constraints and keeps a foothold in fast delivery

claims.claim: A. Launch Parcelbird Now fails every criterion
evidence: Per-order economics: No: −$6.17 median; positive only on plan inputs
Cash need: No: $9.5M to month 18 (plan)
12-month runway rule: No: Breached in month 5; cash out in month 13
Path to profit: No: Only if every driver beats the best observed
Strategic fit: No: Competes with the grocers we sell to; distracts the team
Main risk: Unit economics never close; cash runs out

claims.claim: B. One permanent pilot store fails or partly meets the criteria
evidence: Per-order economics: No: −$6.17 median; −$12.57 pop-up actual
Cash need: Partly: $0.6M capex + ~$2.0M a year loss
12-month runway rule: No: Breached in month 10
Path to profit: No: None: a single store cannot reach scale
Strategic fit: Partly: Little new learning: pop-up and 14-site data already exist
Main risk: Losses with no route to scale

claims.claim: C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers (recommended) meets all criteria
evidence: Per-order economics: Yes: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts
Cash need: Yes: $0.8M a year of hires, phased
12-month runway rule: Yes: Never below 24 months at 60% growth
Path to profit: Yes: Break-even in month 26 (60%) or 36 (40%)
Strategic fit: Yes: Meets demand already in the pipeline
Main risk: ARR growth falls below 34% a year

slides.title: Cash under each option: A runs out in month 13, B drifts to near zero, and C bottoms out at $5.4M before the business turns cash-positive

claims.claim: A runs out in month 13
evidence: A: cash 12 at month 0, 0.07 at month 12, −0.38 at month 13, low of −2.54 at month 22, 0.44 at month 36
A. Launch: Runway < 12 mo. Month 5; Lowest cash −$2.5M

claims.claim: B drifts to near zero
evidence: B: 12 at month 0, low of 0.16 at month 30, 0.87 at month 36
B. Pilot: Runway < 12 mo. Month 10; Lowest cash $0.2M

claims.claim: C bottoms out at $5.4M before the business turns cash-positive
evidence: C: 12 at month 0, low of 5.39 at month 25, 7.54 at month 36
C. Software-first: Runway < 12 mo. Never; Lowest cash $5.4M

claims.claim: Model assumptions
evidence: Today's burn ($0.4M a month) = software opex − gross profit. Opex is held flat apart from the $0.8M hires (in B and C, not in A).
A: $5.4M capex at one store a month (months 1–9), plus the plan's other $4.1M spread evenly over months 1–18 and nothing after. This is the founders' best case.
B: $0.6M capex, then the median store's −$2.0M a year.
Runway = cash ÷ recurring monthly burn.

slides.title: Software-first stays within current cash and the runway rule as long as ARR keeps growing at least 34% a year, just over half today's 60%

claims.claim: Software-first stays within current cash and the runway rule as long as ARR keeps growing at least 34% a year
evidence: 60%: Break-even Month 26; Lowest cash $5.4M; Min. runway 24 mo.
40%: Break-even Month 36; Lowest cash $2.7M; Min. runway 18 mo.
34%: Break-even Month 41; Lowest cash $1.2M; Min. runway 12 mo.
25%: Not by month 48; Runs out; Breached

claims.claim: Break-even ARR
evidence: Break-even ARR = opex ÷ 81% = $8.9M ÷ 0.81 = $11.0M, against $4.1M today.

claims.claim: The pipeline supports the hires
evidence: the 9 late-stage grocers are worth $0.86M of ARR; all 37 are worth $3.55M. The $0.8M of hires pays for itself with 10 contracts (28% of the pipeline).

claims.claim: What has to be true: 34% growth means about 15 net new contracts in year 1, and 60% means about 26. Costs must also stay flat apart from the hires.
evidence: The pack does not give churn or win rates, so phase the hires against signed contracts.

slides.title: The recommendation survives the main uncertainties: most of them would make a launch worse, and the risks to software-first can be managed

claims.claim: Rider minimum-pay rules (2 of 3 cities): Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: +20% rider cost = +$1.48/order at median, +$1.01 on the plan

claims.claim: Density in mid-size Midwest cities: Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: Pop-up 280/day vs median 900; range 400–1,400

claims.claim: Raising AOV could erode the convenience use case: Strengthens "don't launch"
evidence: The plan needs $45 vs $42 best and $31 pop-up

claims.claim: A competitor claims the Midwest first: Low: first-mover status has not created profit
evidence: Incumbents are retreating (QuickBasket −4 cities) and lose money per order

claims.claim: Software growth slows below the minimum: Main risk to C
evidence: Below 34% a year, C breaches the runway rule; 25% runs out of cash

claims.claim: Software cost base grows faster than assumed: Delays C's break-even
evidence: The model holds opex flat apart from the $0.8M of hires

claims.claim: Grocers' own fast delivery competes with our customers: Upside for C
evidence: Several pipeline grocers want store-based fast delivery

slides.title: What would change our mind: reconsider an operator model only when our customers' sites show that the economics work and the funding exists

claims.claim: Trigger 1 – Site-level profit is proven: At least one customer site shows positive contribution after site cost for two consecutive quarters.
evidence: Today: none. Best-observed inputs give −$1.76.

claims.claim: Trigger 2 – The profit drivers are seen at one site at the same time: AOV ≥ $42 and ≥ 3.0 orders per rider-hour at ≥ 1,050 orders a day, or a service fee that does the same job without losing more than 15% of volume.
evidence: Today: no site has both. Break-even with Zipcart's moves needs about 1,042 orders a day.

claims.claim: Trigger 3 – Customers stay: Month-3 retention high enough to repay $38 of acquisition cost within 12 months at actual contribution.
evidence: Today: 22% at 3.1 orders a month, so payback never happens at the median.

claims.claim: Trigger 4 – Funding is ring-fenced: Dedicated capital that leaves the core business with 12 months of runway at all times.
evidence: Today: a new round is "unlikely"; headroom is $7.2M against a $9.5M plan.

claims.claim: Proposed re-entry triggers, reviewed quarterly from the data our software already collects across the 14 customer sites (no extra cost)

slides.title: We ask the board to make four decisions in January 2027 and review progress in 90 days

claims.claim: 1. Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now (Board, Jan 2027)
evidence: Do not commit capex to dark stores and do not extend the pop-up (annualised loss about $1.3M). Keep the pop-up data and cohort learning.

claims.claim: 2. Approve the software scale-up (CEO, Q1 2027)
evidence: 2 engineers and 2 sales hires ($0.8M a year), released in two tranches tied to signed late-stage contracts (9 grocers, $0.86M ARR)

claims.claim: 3. Build a store-based fast-delivery offer (CTO / Sales, Q2 2027)
evidence: Package picking and rider dispatch for grocers who want fast delivery from existing stores; test it with late-stage pipeline accounts

claims.claim: 4. Adopt re-entry triggers and runway reporting (CFO, Q1 2027)
evidence: Quarterly dashboard of the 4 triggers from customer-site data, plus monthly runway against the 12-month rule

claims.claim: 90-day checkpoint (April 2027)
evidence: late-stage conversions against the 9 grocers, pilot interest in store-based fast delivery, actual ARR growth against the 34% minimum, and the first trigger dashboard. If growth is tracking below 34%, hold the second tranche of hires.

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash. Decisions for the board: (1) decline the 2027 launch and do not extend the pop-up; (2) approve the $0.8M a year of software hires, phased against signed contracts; (3) build a store-based fast-delivery offer for the grocers in the pipeline; (4) adopt explicit re-entry triggers, tracked through our customers' sites, before quick commerce is reconsidered.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Launch Parcelbird Now (9 dark stores, 3 cities)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: −$6.17 per order at median, positive only on plan inputs; $9.5M to month 18; runway rule breached in month 5, cash out in month 13; only profitable if every driver beats the best observed; competes with the grocers we sell to and distracts the team.

Rejected: −$6.17 median, −$12.57 pop-up actual; $0.6M capex + ~$2.0M a year loss; runway breached in month 10; a single store cannot reach scale; little new learning since pop-up and 14-site data already exist. Option not in the pack; constructed by the team.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Software-first + store-based fast delivery for grocers
alternatives_considered.treatment: Recommended: 81% gross margin on $96k contracts; $0.8M a year of hires, phased; never below 24 months runway at 60% growth; break-even month 26 (60%) or 36 (40%); meets demand already in the pipeline. Main risk: ARR growth falls below 34% a year.

alternatives_considered.option: Zipcart's moves ($3.99 service fee, promotions cut to 1%) applied to the median store
alternatives_considered.treatment: Still loses $1.05 per order; would need about 1,042 orders a day. A profitable route may exist only at top-quartile density with premium pricing, which is not where a new entrant starts.

normalized.extraction_notes: The deck had no images; every chart came through as data series.
